#20008. The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

📅 16 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1277 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Eater ↗ Open Full Page

The Best Thanksgiving Side Recipes, According to Eater Editors

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1277 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.
  • The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument.
  • According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s massive meal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

The sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

According to recent reports, while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever new ideas have been simmering since last year’s massive meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Industry observers note that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Industry observers note that every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

According to recent reports, why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

Sources indicate that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody claims they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

According to recent reports, while more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

According to recent reports, tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

It has been revealed that this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated quickly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be remarked is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

#20006. Scientists Discover That Producing Light More Slowly Could Improve Future Quantum Networks

Scientists Discover That Producing Light More Slowly Could Improve Future Quantum Networks

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (585 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.
  • Future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons.
  • Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Getting the right light for future quantum networks may depend on what scientists prevent from being emitted, an approach that nearly tripled the share of desired photons.

Future quantum networks may one day allow quantum computers and other devices to exchange information through individual particles of light, known as photons. Making that possible requires reliable sources of photons with carefully controlled properties. One challenge is their frequency, which determines the kind of light they produce. A source can emit photons at several frequencies, leaving only a fraction suitable for the intended connection.

Scientists have traditionally addressed this problem using tiny optical structures called resonators. These structures influence a photon source so that it emits more light at a particular frequency. Although effective, resonators work within a narrow frequency range and must be precisely tuned to each source, making it difficult to use multiple sources together.

Researchers at the Technical University of Munich (TUM) and the Munich Center for Quantum Science and Technology (MCQST) have now demonstrated a different approach. Rather than encouraging a source to produce more light at the desired frequency, they change its surroundings to suppress the frequencies they do not want.

The team uses structures called photonic crystal waveguides, which contain carefully arranged patterns on a nanometer scale. These patterns control the pathways through which light can be emitted, blocking unwanted frequencies while allowing the desired ones to remain.

Recent findings suggest that in initial experiments using erbium, an element already used in fiber-optic technologies, the researchers increased the proportion of photons emitted at the desired frequency from about 23% to around 72%. Previously, achieving comparable results required much more complex resonator systems.

The waveguides also offer greater flexibility. Their larger size allows multiple photon sources, known as emitters, to operate simultaneously within a single device, something that is much more limited with tiny resonators. Because the waveguides work across a broader range of frequencies, researchers can also select the desired frequency without having to precisely tune the structure to each individual emitter.

Another difference is that the latest approach produces photons slightly more slowly, which can actually make them easier to manage.

“If photons are generated too quickly, it’s difficult for us to control their properties,” explains Andreas Reiserer, professor of quantum networks at TUM. “Our approach is therefore significantly better suited for many emitters than the resonators used to date.”.

The findings could help researchers develop the interfaces needed to connect quantum devices over long distances. Such interfaces would have to convert information stored in a quantum system into individual photons that can travel through optical fibers.

Florian Burger, a doctoral student and the publication’s first author, sees the work as an early step toward that goal.

“Quantum networks are expected to connect many quantum systems with one another one day. This requires interfaces that can reliably transfer information from a quantum system to individual photons and then transmit them, for example, via optical fibers. Our work lays the foundation for this.”.

In a recent development, reference: “Inhibited radiative decay enhances single-photon emitters” by Florian Burger, Stephan Rinner, Andreas Gritsch, Kilian Sandholzer and Andreas Reiserer, 16 July 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-75489-5.

It has been revealed that funded by the Federal Ministry of Education and Research (BMBF) and the Free State of Bavaria as part of the federal and state Excellence Strategy. This project was funded by the High-Tech Agenda Bavaria (HTA).

#20005. How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

How the ‘blue tsunami’ crested in North Carolina

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1608 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for upcoming member orientation.
  • LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.
  • In a recent development, but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that north Carolina Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack talks to reporters Sunday at the AC Hotel in Washington as she arrives for upcoming member orientation. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

LaKesha Womack faced towering odds as an underfunded Democrat making her first run for public office in a North Carolina district that Donald Trump carried by 15 points two years ago.

In a recent development, but as early voting surged in mid-October, she sensed she might pull off an upset over Republican Rep. Tim Moore, the influential former speaker of the North Carolina House and a chief architect of the gerrymander that aimed to keep the 14th District safely red.

“There were a lot of pins and needles,” said Womack, a 49-year-old ordained minister who works at a Charlotte-based nonprofit. After seeing long lines at polling places extend into Election Day, she grew more confident: “People were ready to exercise their voice.”.

Womack – who raised less than $60,000 to Moore’s $2.1 million – eked out a 2-point win in the district, which reaches from the Charlotte suburbs to mountain counties in the west.

According to recent reports, saddled with an unpopular president and broad dissatisfaction with the status quo, Republican incumbents across the nation experienced a midterm drubbing last week. As of Monday evening, House Democrats had netted 42 seats, with more races left to be called. The GOP in North Carolina, a state that Trump carried three times, was among the hardest hit.

Democrats have so far flipped five House seats in the Tar Heel State. Besides Womack, the “blue tsunami” also swept in Paul Barringer, a lawyer who founded an outdoor clothing line, and High Point Mayor Cyril Jefferson. And Army veteran Richard Ojeda, who once served in the West Virginia Senate, defeated Rep. Richard Hudson, the chairman of the National Republican Congressional Committee.

Democrats also won two races that had been seen as competitive for much of the cycle. Farmer Jamie Ager flipped an open seat in the state’s mountain west, while Rep. Don Davis held on to his Eastern North Carolina district, which Republicans had redrawn in their favor.

Meanwhile, in the state’s hilly northwest corner, 11-term Republican Virginia Foxx, the chairwoman of the powerful Rules Committee, is fighting for her political future: As of Monday afternoon, former journalist Chuck Hubbard led her by 99 votes in the 5th District, though The Associated Press had yet to call the race.

That was also true in the neighboring 10th District, where GOP incumbent Pat Harrigan had a 1-point edge over Democratic physician associate Ashley Bell. Also uncalled were a pair of contests in Eastern North Carolina, where Republican Rep. Greg Murphy clung to a 233-vote edge over Democratic former state Rep. Raymond Smith and GOP Rep. David Rouzer led Democratic social worker Kimberly Hardy by less than a point.

Recent findings suggest that “Nobody could have predicted this,’’ stated David Wilson Brown, who leads the Democratic Party in Gaston County near Charlotte and has lost two bids for the House, including to Foxx in 2020. “It’s a watershed moment.”.

The Democratic rout in the midterm elections was powered by victories in states with upcoming GOP-favored maps, including Texas, Ohio and Florida.

But Democrats’ success in North Carolina was especially striking given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Since Republicans flipped the state legislature in 2010, and with it control of the redistricting process, no House GOP incumbent had lost a general election in the Tar Heel State until last week.

This year’s  congressional map – the state's sixth in seven election cycles – was engineered by the Republican-led legislature to help the party capture 11 of the state's 14 House seats.

Sources indicate that but the Democratic surge was so big that it easily overpowered the GOP’s built-in edge. Democratic candidates were also lifted by former Gov. Roy Cooper, whose 20-point Senate win provided the underticket with powerful coattails.

“In order for them to gerrymander our state in the way that they did, they were spread very thin,” Brown remarked, referring to state Republicans. “So they were kind of ripe to be defeated that way.”.

The repeated rounds of redistricting may have also erased some of the advantages of incumbency, according to Peter L. Francia, a political science professor at East Carolina University. “If you carve up a district every two years, you've taken away some of that [advantage]. And I think that that came back and hurt Republicans in this cycle.”.

Doug Heye, a GOP strategist and a former spokesman for the Republican National Committee, stated redistricting “ticked off a whole lot of voters, and really activated the Democratic base.”.

On the Republican side, voters were “less motivated because they were unexcited about Trump,’’ Heye added.

Republican incumbents accustomed to winning by comfortable margins weren’t prepared for a political environment driven by anger over the war in Iran and angst about the rising cost of living.

Sources indicate that “Clearly, a lot of those Republicans didn’t take their elections seriously,” Heye said. “They won last time with 18 points. They weren't on anyone's radar screen, so they didn't think they had to do anything.”.

Recent findings suggest that womack credits her win to a grassroots campaign centered on economic issues. While her race wasn’t on the national radar – Moore, after all, won by 16 points in 2024 – and her campaign didn’t have money for ads, she was out in the district doing events every day.

“There are a lot of working families right now who are in the missing middle,” she said in an interview. “They make too much money to get help, but they don't make enough money to get ahead. … Someone who can be working a full-time job, but still doesn’t have enough money to buy groceries or to afford their medications or to have access to health insurance.”.

Womack said her own struggles have shaped her approach to politics. This week, she’s slated to appear in court on a felony charge for allegedly failing to return a rental car in 2019. The incident wound up in one of Moore’s attack ads.

“There are so many people who [understand] what happens when you're down on your luck and you don't have enough money to make good financial decisions,’’ she noted. “Most people don't want those bad decisions to be a definition of their character for the rest of their life.”.

Early in the midterm cycle, Democratic opposition research group American Bridge prepared detailed dossiers on Republican House incumbents in North Carolina.

“Someone like Virginia Foxx, she’s been on the Hill forever,” mentioned Pat Dennis, the group’s president. “She was somebody … who under the radar could be vulnerable. So we started really early.”.

American Bridge’s political arm spent $340,000 on ads targeting Foxx. One spot featured a man who identified himself as a Trump voter expressing anger at the government’s response to Hurricane Helene, which devastated the mountain communities of Western North Carolina two years ago.

Other Democrats scoffed at the group’s decision to spend money targeting entrenched Republicans far from the main House battleground.

“There was a lot of reluctance from people to really believe that that data was correct, but it was,’’ Dennis remarked. “Then over the summer, we saw her numbers collapsing, so we put paid media behind it and it really paid off.”.

Hubbard ran against Foxx two years ago and lost by almost 20 points.

According to recent reports, “I kind of had a notion I was going to do this again,’’ he remarked in an interview Saturday while en route to Washington for freshman orientation. “I don’t like to lose at checkers, much less a congressional race.”.

After a court-drawn map resulted in a split North Carolina delegation after the 2022 elections, state Republicans won back control of the map-making process and went on to win 10 of the state’s 14 House seats under a new map two years later.

At Trump’s urging, Republicans made further tweaks to the North Carolina map last year, but the original gerrymander finally came back to bite the GOP in 2026, according to Hubbard.

According to recent reports, “North Carolina is one of the most severely gerrymandered states,’’ he said. “And what happened was they had to steal from Peter to pay Paul. It's been referred to by political scientists as a dummymander.”.

As the vote count in the 5th District continues, Foxx, whose campaign declined to comment for this story, has requested the presence of nonpartisan election observers.

They “will serve as key, watchful eyes to ensure that this sacred process is not impeded and that all legal votes are counted in a consistent, thorough manner,’’ she posted on social media.

But even before the final races are called, Republicans are already looking to the next election.

Heye, who expects North Carolina to remain a purple state in 2028 and beyond, cautioned the Democrats who won last week not to get too comfortable in Washington. He invoked Fred Heineman, the former Raleigh police chief who rode the 1994 “Republican Revolution” to Congress – and lasted a single term.

“Some of them will lose, and some of the people who lost may run two years from now and get their seat back,’’ he noted.

One GOP operative, who requested anonymity to speak candidly, offered up a similar assessment.

Trump “didn't keep his promises” and that “just got voters very angry and suppressed the GOP base from coming out because, in a midterm election it's a base turnout contest,’’ the strategist said.

“But these Democrats are renting these districts for two years.”.

37 Thanksgiving Cocktails and Drinks for Every Guest

📅 15 Aug 2016 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1511 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle.
  • And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether.
  • Save recipes and proposal every week with confidence.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Whether you’re pouring a cup of cheer or drinking to steel your nerves against Great-Aunt Edna, these Thanksgiving cocktails cover every angle. There are the cranberry, apple, and maple flavors we crave this time of year, plus massive-batch drinks that won’t keep you playing bartender all afternoon. We’re talking freezer-ready martinis, bourbon punch, and a cranberry mule that guests can spike themselves. After all, your to-do list is long enough.

And since Thanksgiving is something of a marathon, we’ve included lighter aperitifs and nonalcoholic drinks for anyone looking to pace themselves—or skip the booze altogether. When dinner gives way to dessert, warm up with a hot buttered rum, mulled wine, or spiced apple cider. Just don’t forget to set out a few Thanksgiving appetizers while you’re at it.

Save recipes and proposal every week with confidence. Download the app.

Recent findings suggest that we love a Paper Plane as much as the next discerning cocktail drinker, but shaking them up one at a time? Hard pass. Batch the bourbon, Aperol, and amaro for this Thanksgiving cocktail ahead, then stir in the lemon juice and water about an hour before serving.

Recent findings suggest that the “upside-down” refers to the inverted ratio of gin and vermouth in these martinis (not what they’ll do to you). The result is a lighter-drinking cocktail you can batch ahead and stash in the freezer until guests arrive.

Sources indicate that all the steeped, spiced flavors you love in a hot toddy, with none of the warmth. This icy twist keeps pre-dinner cocktail hour refreshingly chill. Relatives, take note.

Apple cider, tart cranberry juice, and spicy ginger ale give rum punch a seasonal makeover. Make the cranberry-studded ice cubes ahead of time; they’ll keep the punch cold and make each glass look party-ready.

Sure, a cold beer works fine while you're watching football or tending the turkey fryer. But a pitcher of crisp Mexican lager punched up with margarita citrus makes the occasion feel a little more festive. For another low-effort beer cocktail, try a Spaghett—just lager, Aperol, and lemon.

Sources indicate that for a substantial-batch cocktail with a distinctly autumnal spin, combine rum with dry hard cider and fruit. Prepare the rum base ahead, but save the bubbly cider until just before serving to preserve its fizz.

Bourbon, cognac, floral Earl Grey tea, and an herb-honey syrup make a party-ready punch. For an eye-catching presentation, add an ice ring decorated with lemon slices and rosemary sprigs.

Sources indicate that mezcal, orange liqueur, honey, and chocolate bitters make a lightly smoky cocktail that's particularly good with dessert. Even better, you can batch eight servings and stash them in the freezer up to two weeks ahead. No last-minute shaking required.

Feeling a little gung-ho about Christmas’s fast approach, are we? A major-batch punch packed with cranberry, citrus, nutty sherry, and warming spices makes a delicious bridge between Thanksgiving and the winter holidays.

Industry observers note that A seasonal riff on the French 75 swaps gin for bourbon and adds a homemade pear syrup spiced with cinnamon, ginger, and cloves. We like it for a sparkling toast before dinner or alongside pie afterward.

The season of Hallmark’s flannel-clad himbos calls for a drink to match. Enter this lower-ABV sipper made with apple cider and amaro. A little bitter, a little sweet, and just fizzy enough—rather like the male lead in whatever movie “your aunt” is watching.

Recent findings suggest that homemade cranberry-thyme syrup gives this sparkling cocktail its ruby-red glow. A little Campari adds a pleasantly bitter edge, while Champagne makes it worthy of a holiday toast. The syrup can be prepared up to two weeks ahead.

If you want to start Thanksgiving with a little bubbly, this three-ingredient, lower-ABV aperitif is a fine place to begin. The recipe serves four, and the ginger syrup can be made well in advance.

It has been revealed that replace the gin in a classic Negroni with sparkling wine and you’ve got a lighter, fizzy aperitif. The bubbles mellow Campari’s bitter edge, making this a friendly introduction for the Negroni-curious.

According to recent reports, two ingredients, one very good drink. Fino sherry and ginger ale make a lightly boozy, pleasantly dry cocktail with just enough ginger bite.

Botanical gin, bittersweet grapefruit, and sparkling sake make a bubbly cocktail that’s bright enough to cut through a rich Thanksgiving spread. It serves six, so you can pour a round without mixing drinks one by one.

We love a margarita riff no matter the season. Ginger and rosemary bring a distinctly autumnal edge to this fizzy version, with just enough sparkle to make it feel like a holiday toast.

No punch bowls, cocktail shakers, or complicated mixology required for this two-ingredient drink. You’ve got better things to do between hosting duties and getting all those Thanksgiving sides to the table.

A lower-ABV sipper is your friend during a long day of polite frivolities. The Adonis sounds hella sexy, and we love the earthy nuttiness of sherry and sweet vermouth, made spritzy with club soda.

Sources indicate that on a holiday where cranberries overflow-eth, pour a drink to match. Tart, citrusy, and just sweet enough, this vodka cocktail gets its signature pink hue from cranberry juice. A bright counterpoint to all that rich Thanksgiving food.

According to recent reports, A classic old-fashioned needs just bourbon or rye, sugar, and bitters. Making drinks for a crowd? Follow our massive-batch old-fashioned method to prep ahead and avoid playing bartender all Thanksgiving.

Think of this as an apple-brandy riff on the Manhattan. Sweet vermouth rounds out the fruit’s warmth, making this a particularly fitting fall cocktail.

Industry observers note that not quite a whiskey sour, not quite a cider cocktail, this autumnal drink mixes apple brandy with lemon and orange juices, maple syrup, and a dusting of nutmeg. It tastes like fall without leaning too heavily on baking spices.

Impress your whiskey-loving dad with a Prohibition-era cocktail he may not have heard of. Juicy grapefruit and floral honey give bourbon a bright, citrusy lift, just as winter citrus season is getting underway.

Sources indicate that bourbon, lemon juice, and simple syrup make a tart, boozy drink that’s just sweet enough. It’s ideal for anyone with a minimally stocked bar and a preference for the classics.

Think of the Boulevardier as the Negroni’s bourbon-loving cousin. Whiskey takes the place of gin, bringing warmth and richness to the bittersweet combination of Campari and sweet vermouth. A fine choice for sipping before dinner.

A smoky mezcal cocktail with Earl Grey tea syrup and grapefruit liqueur, this bright, aromatic margarita riff is an intriguing choice for Thanksgiving brunch—or for guests who prefer tequila to bourbon at cocktail hour.

A homemade cranberry-orange jam gives this tequila cocktail a distinctly Thanksgiving twist. Lime juice keeps it tart, while a sugar-salt-and-five-spice rim adds a fragrant finish. Make the jam ahead to streamline cocktail hour.

Recent findings suggest that whether for your Thanksgiving pregame or tomorrow morning’s hair of the dog, a well-made Bloody Mary is always welcome. Worcestershire, horseradish, hot sauce, and fresh lemon give this savory classic its signature kick.

Recent findings suggest that A packed to-do list is no match for this make-ahead drink. Simmer red wine, cider, fruit, and spices ahead of time, then add tawny port and gently reheat when your guests arrive. Keep it warm in a slow cooker for self-service away from the kitchen.

Sources indicate that we’d welcome a pot of mulled apple cider at any fall gathering. It’s nonalcoholic, serves a crowd, and fills the kitchen with the scent of warming spices. Guests can add a tipple of brandy, bourbon, Calvados, or rum if they wish.

Can’t decide between hot cider and spice-rich chai? Have both. This cozy, nonalcoholic drink brings tea and warming spices to apple cider, making it a particularly good companion for a second slice of pie.

Recent findings suggest that for those who’d rather drink their Thanksgiving dessert, a warm mug of dark rum, butter, sugar, and spices delivers the goods. It’s rich, fragrant, and an excellent reason to linger at the table after the pie plates are cleared.

It has been revealed that blood orange, ginger, cinnamon, and cloves make this sweet-tart, nonalcoholic drink feel right at home on Thanksgiving. Prepare the shrub ahead, then top with sparkling water when guests arrive.

Who says a nonalcoholic spritz can’t have a little attitude? A bittersweet alcohol-free aperitif and a splash of olive brine give this savory, citrusy drink plenty of complexity. Serve it very cold, with an olive garnish.

Recent findings suggest that green tea, lemon juice, fresh mint, and honey make a soothing tonic after the Thanksgiving bacchanal. Alcohol-free on its own, it can take a splash of mezcal if anyone wants to steer it into cocktail territory.

Industry observers note that spiced maple syrup and cranberry juice reimagine the typical Moscow mule as a Thanksgiving drink that skips the vodka. Note that Angostura bitters contain alcohol; for a completely alcohol-free version, use an alternative like All the Bitter.

ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (974 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • Industry observers note that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

Industry observers note that the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

To help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

However, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

It has been revealed that but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

It has been revealed that crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

In a recent development, but ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.

#20002. Tech Report: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

Tech Report: The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5301 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • According to recent reports, this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

According to recent reports, this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

Recent findings suggest that we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Industry observers note that latest to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

Sources indicate that the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

It has been revealed that this guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most notable restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

According to recent reports, we update this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Recent findings suggest that new to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Sources indicate that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he launched Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

In a recent development, mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

In a recent development, this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

In a recent development, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the new template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

Industry observers note that these days, London has no shortage of excellent fresh-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

East Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

This quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

Recent findings suggest that the area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The latest online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Industry observers note that chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

It has been revealed that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Latest York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

After a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

It has been revealed that clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

According to recent reports, while the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most notable British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

According to recent reports, joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

Given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

According to recent reports, chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand new, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Sources indicate that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

It has been revealed that shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Industry observers note that bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

For my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy upcoming surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

It has been revealed that chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Sources indicate that mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a big group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

There’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

Industry observers note that A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

According to recent reports, this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

Recent findings suggest that in his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

The second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Sources indicate that bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in latest-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

According to recent reports, fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

Despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

#20001. Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

Scientists Uncover Why a Common Nutrient Can Be Dangerous for Blood Vessels

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with key implications for people with chronic kidney disease.
  • It has been revealed that A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans.
  • It has been revealed that the study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an vital regulator of blood phosphate levels.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New research suggests that dietary phosphate may influence blood vessel damage and lifespan, with key implications for people with chronic kidney disease.

It has been revealed that A newly identified role for a protein in the kidneys could help explain why excess phosphate in the blood contributes to hardened arteries and shorter lifespans. Researchers at the University of Colorado Anschutz School of Medicine found that animals lacking this protein developed more calcium deposits in their blood vessels and died earlier, particularly when consuming a diet high in phosphate.

It has been revealed that the study, published in October 2026, identified TMEM174 as an vital regulator of blood phosphate levels. Reducing dietary phosphate lessened some of the harmful effects in animals deficient in the protein. The findings point to a potential treatment target for chronic kidney disease (CKD), a condition that makes it difficult for the body to eliminate excess phosphate.

Recent findings suggest that the kidneys continuously filter phosphate from the bloodstream, removing excess amounts through urine while retaining enough to support essential functions such as bone formation. A protein called NPT2A helps maintain this balance by reabsorbing approximately three-quarters of the filtered phosphate and returning it to the blood.

In a recent development, the researchers discovered that TMEM174 acts as a counterbalance to NPT2A. By binding to NPT2A and reducing its activity, TMEM174 helps prevent excessive phosphate reabsorption. In animal models lacking TMEM174, phosphate regulation became disrupted, vascular calcification increased, and lifespan was significantly reduced.

“We don’t fully understand how yet, but somehow TMEM174 is destabilizing NPT2A,” says Makoto Miyazaki, PhD, a research professor in the Division of Renal Diseases and Hypertension and senior author of the study. “And without enough TMEM174, homeostasis is disrupted.”.

In a recent development, phosphorus is an essential nutrient found in meat, fish, dairy products, nuts, legumes, and whole grains. It is also commonly added to processed foods and beverages to improve flavor and extend shelf life. Unlike many naturally occurring phosphorus compounds, phosphate additives are generally absorbed more efficiently by the digestive system.

In a recent development, although the body needs phosphorus, persistently elevated blood phosphate (hyperphosphatemia) can damage the cardiovascular system. Excess phosphate can cause smooth muscle cells in blood vessel walls to develop characteristics of bone-forming cells. These altered cells promote the accumulation of calcium phosphate crystals, causing blood vessels to stiffen (or calcify).

Healthy arteries expand and contract in response to changing blood flow. Calcification reduces that flexibility, contributing to vascular aging and increasing cardiovascular risks. In the latest study, the combination of TMEM174 deficiency and a phosphate-rich diet accelerated this process in animals.

According to recent reports, “Phosphate is really underestimated in terms of longevity in all mammals. The higher the concentration of phosphate in the blood, the shorter the lifespan,” claims Miyazaki.

According to recent reports, elevated blood phosphate is relatively uncommon in the general population because healthy kidneys can usually remove the excess. In people with CKD, however, declining kidney function reduces phosphate excretion, allowing the mineral to accumulate in the bloodstream.

This impaired phosphate regulation can contribute to vascular calcification, which is particularly common in people with kidney disease. The newly discovered role of TMEM174 suggests another potential source of vulnerability. Although TMEM174 deficiency appears to be primarily genetic rather than caused by CKD, researchers suspect that people affected by both conditions could face additional cardiovascular risks.

According to recent reports, the experiments established a connection between TMEM174 deficiency, abnormal phosphate regulation, vascular calcification, and reduced survival in animal models. Whether differences in TMEM174 activity have comparable effects on cardiovascular health or lifespan in humans remains to be determined.

The findings suggest that treatments affecting TMEM174 or its interaction with NPT2A might help the kidneys eliminate more phosphate instead of returning it to the bloodstream. Such an approach could eventually provide another way to manage phosphate levels in people with CKD.

Dietary changes may also help. The researchers found that reducing phosphate intake partially protected animals lacking TMEM174 from harmful effects. Miyazaki notes that limiting phosphate-rich processed foods, including fast food, deli meats, and sodas, could be beneficial. However, phosphate occurs naturally in so many foods that dietary restrictions alone may be insufficient, particularly for people with impaired kidney function.

Future research will examine how TMEM174 interacts with other proteins and hormones involved in phosphate regulation. Miyazaki also hopes to investigate why calcium deposits are so prevalent in the blood vessels of people with CKD.

“Scientists have been studying phosphate homeostasis for over 100 years, so to still find a upcoming protein that regulates phosphate is kind of unique,” says Miyazaki.

Sources indicate that reference: “TMEM174 deficiency reduces longevity by promoting phosphate-driven vascular calcification” by Jose G. Miranda, Judith Blaine and Makoto Miyazaki, 2 October 2026, Scientific Reports. DOI: 10.1038/s41598-026-74353-2.
