After two years with nearly 100 measles outbreaks, thousands sickened and nearly a dozen deaths, the United States has officially lost its measles elimination status.

According to recent reports, the highly contagious disease is now endemic in the United States, the Pan American Health Organization declared November 17. Analyses of cases dated from when the first outbreak began in 2025 in West Texas through part of 2026 revealed the virus has been spreading uninterrupted for more than a year. That benchmark signals measles is no longer under control.

Industry observers note that the United States is not alone. Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status, PAHO announced; Canada had lost it in 2025. “Measles is resurging globally amid persistent gaps in vaccination coverage,” PAHO director Jarbas Barbosa said in a Nov. 17 news conference. “And this global trend is also affecting the Americas.” Countries will need to not only stop ongoing outbreaks, but also prove that no one caught measles within their borders for a full year to regain measles-free status.

Recent findings suggest that that won’t happen overnight. But there is a way, experts say. Vaccinating people across the country, particularly in areas with low vaccination rates, will stifle the virus’s spread. But so far, the U.S. federal public health response has taken a back seat to efforts from state and local health departments to curb ongoing outbreaks.

Measles’s return “is an enormous black eye on the reputation of the United States,” stated epidemiologist Jennifer Nuzzo of the Brown University School of Public Health in Providence, R.I., in a Nov. 9 webinar hosted by the university. The Americas led the global campaign to control the virus, and in 2016 the region became the first to eliminate measles transmission from all its countries.

Industry observers note that “To lose [elimination status] means we’re going backwards… meaning decades of progress lost,” Nuzzo said. “It’s an indicator of our lack of protection. It is an indicator of our lack of preparedness for disease threats in general.”.

PAHO’s verdict comes amid a surge of measles not seen in the United States since 1991. Health officials have recorded more than 7,000 cases since the beginning of the West Texas outbreak. That tally includes nearly 2,300 measles cases in 2025 and 5,412 in 2026 as of November 12, according to the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. Over 90 percent of cases have been in people who are unvaccinated or whose status is unknown. States report that 13 people have died, although the CDC so far recognizes only nine of those deaths.

Sources indicate that while mild measles symptoms include high fever, cough and a rash, roughly 1 in 5 people will be hospitalized with complications such as pneumonia or brain swelling. Children younger than 5 years and adults over 20 are more likely to get sick, as are pregnant women and their infants. At least 13 babies were born infected, called congenital measles, since the beginning of 2025, researchers report November 16 in NEJM Evidence. Those babies are at risk for developing dangerous brain swelling that is almost always fatal later on in life.

In a recent development, the measles, mumps and rubella, or MMR, vaccine helped eliminate measles from the United States in 2000. After that, cases still sometimes popped up. Those cases were mostly in unvaccinated people traveling from parts of the world where the virus still widely circulates. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent outbreaks.

But widespread misinformation, including a disproven claim that the vaccine causes autism, means fewer children are receiving the MMR shot and more people are questioning its safety. According to the CDC, roughly 92 percent of kindergarteners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in 2025, down from 95 percent in 2019. And in 2025, 83 percent of U.S. adults viewed the MMR vaccine as safe, down from 86 percent in 2024, according to a survey from the University of Pennsylvania’s Annenberg Public Policy Center. Yet decades of evidence show the vaccine is safe and highly effective.

It has been revealed that that measles made a comeback is not a surprise, says Nathan Lo, an infectious diseases physician and epidemiologist at Stanford University School of Medicine. Until recently, outbreaks were largely isolated to communities with low vaccination rates and rapidly contained. But now, outbreaks seem to be more likely to spill over into neighboring communities, Lo says. “There’s a lot of potential connectedness between the outbreaks.”.

In a recent development, what’s more, some infected people aren’t getting tested, making them invisible to officials who are now struggling to trace chains of transmission. An outbreak that hit Arizona and Utah, for instance, was far larger than official numbers suggest, researchers reported July 15 in a preprint at medRxiv.org. The roughly 1,000 confirmed cases may represent just 20 to 30 percent of the outbreak’s true size.

Industry observers note that A functional surveillance system is crucial to keeping outbreaks under control, Jonathan Temte, a family medicine physician at the University of Wisconsin School of Medicine and Public Health in Madison, stated in the Brown University webinar. Without good surveillance across the entire country, “we can miss pockets out there if people aren’t reporting, if people are hiding cases.”.

Sources indicate that but surveillance alone won’t stop the virus from “popcorning across the country,” Nuzzo stated. “Measles has returned, and it’s going to take vaccination to stop it.”.

Over the last two years, measles outbreaks have popped up across the United States, sickening thousands of people since mid-January 2025. Most of those cases, shown by county where they were reported, are in people who are unvaccinated. Colors on the map indicate the relative number of cases reported. Green represents the lowest and red the highest number of cases. Notable outbreaks have appeared in Utah, Arizona, Texas, South Carolina, Wisconsin and Pennsylvania.

Michael Mitchell and Andrea Uhlig/Brown University School of Public Health.

In a recent development, efforts to boost vaccine uptake could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles, but not all. “Figuring out which ones are [high risk] can be a little tricky,” Lo states. “But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

Homing in on school districts or individual schools could also help. State health departments typically report vaccination rates among school-age children by county. But that broad metric can hide high risk schools with low vaccination rates, epidemiologists Siyu Chen and Ana Bento reported in August in Nature Medicine. Computer simulations relying on data that included 50,000 schools across the United States showed that school-level estimates best revealed where the virus could gain a foothold. That was true even if county-level vaccination rates were close to 95 percent.

Recent findings suggest that another element that influenced where measles took off was whether communities with cases were near other areas with low vaccination rates, the team found. The outbreak in Texas, for instance, may have ended faster because communities with low vaccination rates were farther away from one another compared with outbreaks in South Carolina and Pennsylvania, states Bento, of Cornell University. Neighboring areas where many are unvaccinated may face longer-burning outbreaks. “Which is what we are now seeing,” Bento says.

It has been revealed that measles elimination status can be regained. The declaration that the virus is endemic is “not a punishment,” Bento says. It’s a sign that something needs to change. That might include vaccine catch-up campaigns, community outreach or getting rid of nonmedical vaccine exemptions.

Industry observers note that local public health officials are “doing every last thing that you can imagine with limited resources,” health psychologist Noel T. Brewer mentioned in a Nov. 12 webinar hosted by the Association of Health Care Journalists. But a cohesive blueprint at the federal level could bolster defenses before the virus arrives in new states, noted Brewer, of the University of North Carolina Gillings School of Global Public Health in Chapel Hill.

Such efforts could be targeted toward areas with low vaccination rates. Most places across the United States still have vaccination rates high enough to fend off measles. “A subset [with low vaccination rates] are high risk,” Lo states. “Figuring out which ones are which can be a little tricky. But if you do, then intervening in those places can be quite helpful to mitigate spread.”.

It has been revealed that there’s also wiggle room in the childhood vaccine schedule to provide kids extra protection. Normally children don’t get their first MMR dose until their first birthday. But doctors can give infants an extra MMR dose at 6 months if there is an active outbreak in their area. Pediatricians can also offer the second dose a month after the first one, rather than waiting until around the time children start kindergarten. Adults, particularly those who received only one dose, can also get a booster. It’s unclear whether health officials will officially recommend such actions.

Sources indicate that “The problem is that there’s no trusted source for this vaccine decision anymore,” Lo indicates. Previous vaccine recommendations were up to the CDC’s Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices, which was disbanded in March after lawsuits blocked appointments made by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. “Now, there’s a lot of different medical societies and initiatives to try and fill that void,” Lo says. But it’s unclear which would be best positioned to lead.

CDC director Erica Schwartz has mentioned the health agency will not be changing its response to ongoing outbreaks. “We’re going to be doing the same exact thing that we’ve been doing today, which is working with the states,” she told Reuters. The CDC did not respond to Science News requests for an interview, but shared in a Nov. 17 statement that the agency will “encourage MMR vaccination, expand access to vaccines, and help communities close gaps in protection.”.

It has been revealed that eliminating measles again will take dedicated resources and more funding funneled to public health departments across the country, Lo indicates. “You see increasing measles outbreaks and a lot of time and resources to contain these outbreaks at a time where you’re slashing budgets,” Lo says, “that’s a really bad mismatch.”.

Public health responses to measles are expensive. Officials in Fresh Mexico spent an estimated $5.4 million — over $53,000 per case — responding to a 2025 outbreak that was linked to West Texas. The CDC has provided an additional $100 million to states to help fight measles.

Sources indicate that other countries have beaten back measles after an unwelcome return. Extensive vaccination campaigns helped Venezuela and Brazil regain measles elimination status after briefly losing it in 2017 and 2019. The Public Health Agency of Canada also revealed that its nearly two-year-long outbreak officially ended in October, though it’s unclear when the country might earn its status back.

In a recent development, “It is not hopeless,” Nuzzo said. “It can be done, and I hope it will be done [in the United States].”.

#19887. Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1402 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Cattails send oxygen into marsh mud, where it can change the soil chemistry

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in.
  • The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud.
  • Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that cattails grow in mud with almost no oxygen, but their roots bring some in. A latest study found that growing roots release oxygen even at night.

The roots of cattails can grow in oxygen-poor marsh mud. To keep these roots alive, the plant carries air down from its leaves.

Part of that oxygen then escapes into the surrounding mud.

According to recent reports, it has generally been assumed that this leak occurs mostly in daylight. During the day, the leaves produce oxygen and their pores stay open to the air.

A laboratory study of narrowleaf cattails has found that daylight altered the leak only slightly. Instead, oxygen appeared wherever a new root or underground stem was growing. It remained there through the night as well.

The findings suggest that the season of root growth may matter more for marsh chemistry than the time of day.

The study was conducted by Ilana Stein and Zoe Cardon of the Ecosystems Center. This center is part of the Marine Biological Laboratory (MBL) in Woods Hole, Massachusetts.

It has been revealed that four plants were examined one at a time in boxes of marsh mud. No measurements were made in a marsh itself.

Sources indicate that flooding leaves the soil of a wetland without oxygen. Most wetland plants cope with this through spongy tissue in their leaves, stems and roots that is filled with air.

Sources indicate that this tissue serves as a kind of snorkel for the plant. Oxygen travels through it from the air above the water to the root tips below.

Recent findings suggest that narrowleaf cattail is particularly well adapted to flooded ground. Air spaces were found by earlier studies to make up as much as 74% of its leaf tissue.

In the roots, the figure reached as much as 32%.

Some of the oxygen that arrives is used by the roots and the rest can leak away. This leaked oxygen allows microbes that depend on it to survive in mud where they otherwise could not.

Certain microbes consume methane before the gas can enter the plant and escape through its leaves. Others break down organic matter in the mud and could reduce how much carbon the soil stores.

The same leak is also valuable to people. Cattails are planted in constructed wetlands that treat wastewater and are used to clean up contaminated soil. Both of these uses rely on the oxygen released by their roots.

Cattails and mud were collected by Stein and Cardon from a marsh along the Parker River in northeastern Massachusetts. This marsh forms part of the Plum Island Ecosystems Long Term Ecological Research program.

Each plant was placed in a narrow clear plastic box filled with live mud from the same marsh. The box measured about 15.5 inches tall and 8 inches wide (39 by 20 centimeters).

Much of one inside wall was covered with a film containing a dye that responds to oxygen. A camera photographed the film under blue light.

The colors in every image indicated how much oxygen was present in the mud behind the film.

These films were made by hand by Suzanne Thomas, who works as a senior research assistant at MBL.

Images were captured every few minutes over periods that usually lasted two to three days.

The box itself remained in darkness behind black cloth. Meanwhile, the leaves grew outside under a lamp that was switched on from 5 a.m. to 7 p.m.

It has been revealed that A sensor attached to one leaf collected readings once every minute. It recorded how quickly the leaf absorbed carbon dioxide and how widely its pores had opened.

The team could therefore compare the activity of the leaves with the oxygen in the mud.

Mud that held no roots also held no oxygen. This changed as soon as part of a cattail grew into it.

It has been revealed that cattails spread by means of horizontal underground stems known as rhizomes. Newly introduced roots then emerge from these stems.

Whenever a new rhizome or root entered a patch of mud, the oxygen level there rose rapidly from zero. It climbed to between 25% and 35% of the amount found in water that is fully saturated with air.

This oxygen did not persist for long. Around a rhizome, it disappeared after about three days on average. Around a main root, it lasted about four days.

According to recent reports, according to the authors, a seal may be partly responsible. Older sections of a cattail root develop a barrier that is thought to keep oxygen inside. This would allow more of it to reach the growing tip.

Stein and Cardon wrote that this barrier and the steady demand for oxygen in the mud may explain the decline.

Sources indicate that in many cases, oxygen returned to the mud a second time. Fine side roots broke through the sealed surface of a main root and oxygen spread through the mud around them.

According to recent reports, these later pools of oxygen persisted for about three weeks on average. In one plant, they lasted longer than five weeks.

An earlier study had found that cattail side roots do not develop the barrier that seals a main root.

As a result, a single root released oxygen into the mud on two occasions. The first release lasted a few days near the tip and the second continued for weeks along the sides.

Industry observers note that earlier studies of rice and a salt marsh cordgrass had reported strong control of the leak by day and night. In the cattails, light did have some effect and this was mostly seen around the side roots.

Across three plants, the gap between the highest and lowest oxygen levels of each day averaged about 3% of saturation. No daily pattern could be detected in the fourth plant.

New growth therefore changed oxygen levels far more than the cycle of day and night.

The oxygen in the mud also did not follow the activity of the leaves. It increased during the first two to three hours of light. For the rest of the day, it declined even though the leaves were becoming more active.

Recent findings suggest that after the lights were turned off, the oxygen fell for about two hours. It then rose slowly until the following morning.

Industry observers note that mud consumes oxygen swiftly on its own. Oxygen-rich water was injected into mud that held no roots. The oxygen was gone within about an hour and a half.

The roots must therefore have continued to release oxygen in the dark.

The authors wrote that it remains unclear how cattails achieve this without exhausting the oxygen in their own air spaces.

One explanation they proposed is that the leaf pores did not close completely at night. Air could then have continued to enter the plant.

Methane, soil carbon, and microbes were not examined in the study.

In a recent development, the study also followed just four plants of a single species. None of them was kept in its box for more than two months.

If growth is what controls the oxygen, then the next question is when cattails grow underground.

Sources indicate that stein is a postdoctoral researcher in Cardon’s lab. She noted the results turned the team’s attention to the timing of root growth across the year.

Earlier field data and models suggest that cattail rhizomes gain the most mass in mid to late summer. This follows the expansion of the leaves.

The authors wrote that oxygen from newly introduced rhizomes and their roots may be especially intense during that period.

Methane is released by wetlands naturally and oxygen around roots can reduce it.

“Natural greenhouse gas emissions have been happening forever,” said Cardon, a senior scientist at MBL.

She noted the team hopes to identify natural processes that could act as levers on those emissions.

Sources indicate that the cattails were not followed through a complete growing season or observed in a marsh. The authors wrote that understanding when rhizomes and roots grow through the year should become a priority.

In their view, such knowledge is needed to understand the chemistry of marshes where cattails dominate.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

#19884. Some patients who appear unresponsive can control a computer with their thoughts

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Some patients who appear unresponsive can control a computer with their thoughts

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1064 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • One in three ICU patients who appeared comatose changed a beeping tone by thinking, and that sign of hidden consciousness predicted recovery.
  • Industry observers note that after a severe brain injury, a patient may show no visible response when doctors ask them to move.
  • In a Latest York intensive care unit, 13 of 41 patients who appeared unresponsive changed how fast a sound beeped by trying to open and close a hand.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

One in three ICU patients who appeared comatose changed a beeping tone by thinking, and that sign of hidden consciousness predicted recovery.

Industry observers note that after a severe brain injury, a patient may show no visible response when doctors ask them to move. But their brain waves can sometimes reveal that they’re following the command.

In a Latest York intensive care unit, 13 of 41 patients who appeared unresponsive changed how fast a sound beeped by trying to open and close a hand.

In a recent development, electrodes on the scalp recorded the patients’ brain waves. A bedside computer detected signals linked to the attempted movement and adjusted the beeping the patients heard through headphones.

The 13 who could do it were also far more likely to regain consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, they were far more likely to be able to look after themselves for hours at a time.

Jan Claassen, a professor of neurology at Columbia University’s Vagelos College of Physicians and Surgeons, led the study.

He also runs the neurocritical care unit at NewYork-Presbyterian and Columbia University Irving Medical Center, where the patients were treated.

In a recent development, in a 2019 study, his team recorded brain waves while unresponsive patients were told to open and close a hand. A computer program found that about 15% of them were trying to comply.

Some patients highlighted brain activity consistent with following a command even though they did not visibly move. Researchers call this cognitive motor dissociation.

“Our brain-computer interface is only a first step, but it demonstrates that, in principle, we could hopefully in the future give some of these patients a voice,” Claassen said.

Most brain-computer interfaces that let paralyzed people type, play games, or move a robotic arm use a chip implanted on the brain, and they need long training.

Neither suits someone who was healthy last week and isn’t responding now.

So the team used the 21 EEG electrodes already glued to each patient’s scalp.

Through headphones, a recorded voice said “to make the beep sound faster, keep opening and closing your right hand,” then “to make the beep sound slower, stop opening and closing your right hand.”.

A bedside computer read the brain waves as they came in and changed the beeps when it detected the effort.

Each session was two five-minute practice rounds, during which the program learned that patient’s signals, and then a ten-minute test with no help.

The voice encouraged patients when the beeps changed and congratulated them when they hit the target.

It has been revealed that the 41 patients were tested a median of five days after their injuries. Their median age was 65, and most had suffered a stroke, a brain bleed, a cardiac arrest, or a head injury.

Sources indicate that thirteen of the 41 patients, or 32%, passed the test on at least one try. Six of them did it within the first week after their injury, which surprised the researchers.

In a recent development, for comparison, all eight healthy volunteers controlled the tone, and so did nine of 22 conscious patients in the same unit. The conscious patients who failed were mostly sedated, agitated, or unable to speak after a stroke.

The unresponsive patients who succeeded were slow. Their brain signals demonstrated up about 50 seconds after each instruction.

In a recent development, conscious patients took about 17 seconds and healthy volunteers about 15. A patient who looks like they are ignoring a command may simply be answering it late.

Recent findings suggest that each patient also took the team’s older command-following exam, the one from 2019. Eight of the 41 passed it. Every one of those who was tested on the tone the same day could control it.

But nine of the 33 patients who failed the older exam could control the tone anyway.

The authors wrote that the beeping feedback may simply be more engaging than a voice repeating the same command.

“EEG is used in clinical practice every day in the ICU,” Claassen mentioned.

“The only sophisticated part is the computer program we wrote, which analyzes the data in real time and modulates the feedback to the patient.”.

Four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone regained consciousness before leaving the hospital.

Among the 28 patients who could not control the beeping, only one had regained consciousness by hospital discharge.

A year later, six of the 13, or 46%, could be left alone for at least eight hours a day without help. Two of the 28 others, or 7%, could. Patients who had failed both tests did worst of all.

According to recent reports, of those 24 patients, not one recovered that much. By then 17 of the 41 had died, 14 of them after life support was withdrawn.

The deaths after withdrawal are why the authors wrote at length about ethics.

According to recent reports, four of the 13 patients who controlled the tone died after life support was withdrawn. The authors cautioned that a negative result cannot rule out awareness.

The study covered one hospital and 41 patients with very different injuries, some of them sedated during testing.

Patients who recovered were also examined more often, which could have made recovery easier to spot in them. The authors wrote that the result needs repeating at other centers before it guides care.

In a recent development, controlling a tone is also not talking. The study didn’t try to get a yes or a no from anyone. The authors wrote that doing so may need a level of awareness beyond what this test detects.

Families and the conscious patients were asked what they wanted.

All 37 who answered supported the idea, and they asked for a loved one’s voice in place of the recording, and for ways to signal pain, hunger, or simple awareness.

“Our goal is to refine the system so that patients can tell their doctors and loved ones how they are feeling – if they are in pain or hungry, for instance – with more direct communication,” Claassen said.

For some patients who highlighted no visible response at the bedside, the beeps offered evidence that they could follow a command.

The full study was published in the journal Brain.

#19883. Tech Report: Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1279 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Meerkats cross the desert together, but what happens when one finds itself alone?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1279 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.
  • Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group.
  • In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Researchers tracked 20 meerkats in the Kalahari Desert to see how they navigated familiar territory after being separated from their groups.

Meerkats leave their burrows together each morning and forage as a group. How well can one find its way alone?

In South Africa’s Kalahari Desert, researchers carried 20 adult meerkats up to 0.9 miles from where they caught them.

It has been revealed that after release, 18 reached a familiar spot or found their group. Fourteen headed first to the burrow where the group had slept.

The team found no clear advantage for older or more experienced animals.

The researchers suggest that daily group travel may give meerkats enough experience to navigate alone.

The study was led by Mathilde Martin of the University of Zurich. The team worked alongside the Kalahari Meerkat Project, which follows about 15 wild groups accustomed to people.

The project is run from the Kalahari Research Centre, which is known as the KRC.

“At the KRC, our work with meerkats allows us to distract them with a water bottle and fit their collar in a few seconds while they stand upright drinking; a mere formality for them,” Martin noted.

A GPS tag on each collar logged the position of the animal once every second. A radio transmitter was also fitted, along with a small audio recorder for the meerkat’s calls.

It has been revealed that the team tested a total of 20 adults from five groups between January and March 2025. Fifteen of these animals were male, whereas only five of them were female.

Each meerkat was caught while its group was foraging and was released up to 0.9 miles (1.5 kilometers) away.

Such a distance is greater than the ground usually covered by a meerkat group in a whole day.

Sources indicate that the release sites were located inside the territory of each group. The team chose areas that the group had not visited for at least 30 days.

Homing experiments of this kind have previously been carried out on honeybees and desert ants. Highly social animals that travel in tight groups have rarely been tested in the same way.

This is because the knowledge of one animal is difficult to separate from the decisions of the group.

Eighteen of the 20 meerkats left the release site. The sleeping burrow, the capture spot or the group itself was reached by all 18 of them.

Some of the meerkats departed almost at once, whereas others circled the release site for nearly 90 minutes.

The area covered by them ranged from half an acre to almost 17 acres (2,050 to 68,200 square meters).

A meerkat rarely strayed from its course once a direction had been chosen. Sixteen of the animals aimed for a fixed place.

The sleeping burrow was visited first by 14 of those 16.

On average, the straight-line distance to the target amounted to 82% of the distance actually walked by the meerkat.

The release areas had not been visited by the group for a month. The team therefore concluded that the meerkats had been navigating from long-term memory.

It has been revealed that two males never left the release site, and they were carried back to their groups after 90 minutes. They were no younger or less experienced than the others.

The authors suspect that stress kept them there, and not a lack of knowledge.

Recent findings suggest that some meerkats had been expected to navigate better than others. Subordinate males sometimes leave the group and go alone in search of mates.

Other females are occasionally driven out for a while by the dominant female.

Solo trips of this kind could be counted as practice. The researchers also considered the age of each animal, together with the time it spent on guard duty.

Attention was given as well to how often it scent-marked the territory or dug at shelters.

None of those traits predicted how long a meerkat explored. Neither did they predict how accurately it set off or how straight it travelled.

No clear difference was found between males and females either, although only five females took part.

Recent findings suggest that the authors think that the explanation lies in the territory itself. It is small and stable, with 0.3 to 0.6 miles (0.5 to 1 kilometer) covered by a group daily.

The whole territory has probably been crossed several times by each member by the time adulthood is reached.

The authors wrote that pigeons of different ages are likewise able to find their way home equally well.

According to recent reports, on the way home, the meerkats spent about two-thirds of their time searching for cues. Most of the remaining time was spent moving.

Few of them stopped to eat, and those that did only grabbed millipedes crawling on the sand.

According to recent reports, the animals stood upright or climbed a bush or tree trunk in order to scan the landscape. Overall, they spent 10 times longer on looking than on sniffing.

In a recent development, this balance between looking and sniffing was altered late in the trip. By that stage, a meerkat had reached its target and was searching for its group. Sniffing then took up more than 20% of its cue-searching time.

Along the way, meerkats were often seen sniffing around boltholes. These are the small shelters that the animals dig across their territory. An earlier experiment had found that meerkats remember where their boltholes are.

The authors suggested that boltholes may serve as landmarks in a meerkat’s memory of its territory.

The search was not ended by reaching the burrow, because the group could have moved on since the capture.

Thirteen of the 20 meerkats rejoined their groups on their own. The slowest took almost three hours.

The burrow or the capture site was reached by five others. The group had nevertheless not been found by them when the three-hour limit ran out.

These animals were caught again and returned by the team.

According to recent reports, the researchers could not explain why some meerkats succeeded while others did not. Success was not predicted by a straighter trip to the burrow.

Nor was it predicted by the number of scent marks left behind by the group.

Industry observers note that the tracking of a group was compared by the authors to a predator following its prey. The target keeps moving and its route is not known to the searcher.

It has been revealed that twenty animals make up a small sample, as the authors wrote. All of them were subordinate adults older than 10 months, so pups and dominant animals were not tested.

According to recent reports, every release was also made inside familiar territory. The results therefore do not show how a meerkat would manage in a place it does not know.

Industry observers note that two reasons for looking around could not be fully separated either. A lone meerkat that scans the landscape may be checking for predators as much as searching for landmarks.

If many group members know the territory, the next question is who leads when the group moves.

The authors want to know whether certain traits influence which animal takes the lead. The physical needs of an animal and its social rank are two examples.

Co-author Benjamin Robira stated the team now wants to understand what makes up a meerkat’s mental picture of its territory.

The researchers also intend to study how the animals get from one point to another.

The full study was published in the Journal of Experimental Biology.

Satellites watched a cluster of thunderstorms become Cyclone Xavier

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite images show how promptly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.
  • Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite images show how promptly Tropical Cyclone Xavier developed a distinct eye as it strengthened near the northern Cook Islands.

Today’s Image of the Day features Tropical Cyclone Xavier spinning over the South Pacific near the northern Cook Islands.

Bands of white clouds curve around the storm’s eye. In satellite images from a few hours earlier, the eye was still forming.

The MODIS instrument aboard NASA’s Aqua satellite captured this scene at 4:53 p.m. Cook Islands time on November 16, 2026.

By then, Xavier’s strongest sustained winds were estimated at about 120 miles per hour.

The clouds would tighten around a storm that was still gaining strength.

A few days earlier, the system that became Xavier was a loose cluster of thunderstorms.

In microwave satellite images from November 14, its structure was hard to make out.

By late November 16, distinct rainbands curved around a well-defined eye.

A separate sequence from the GOES-18 weather satellite indicates the eye becoming easier to pick out over the course of hours.

The difference between those views comes down to what each instrument can see.

A daylight image like this one highlights sunlight reflected by clouds and the ocean.

High clouds can hide the circulation beneath them, making it difficult to tell where a developing storm is centered.

Microwave observations can reveal parts of the rain structure beneath those clouds, giving forecasters another way to follow a storm as it organizes.

The eye is typically the calmest part of a mature tropical cyclone. Air sinks there, which helps keep clouds from forming.

Just outside it, warm, moist air rises in a ring of thunderstorms called the eyewall. That ring is usually where the storm’s strongest winds are found.

Farther from the center, the sweeping bands visible from space can bring bursts of heavy rain and wind, with quieter stretches in between.

Someone on an island can experience several rounds of rough weather as successive bands pass overhead, even when the eye stays out at sea.

From above, the bands look like parts of a single spiral. On the ground, they can feel like a series of separate storms.

In a recent development, the ocean beneath Xavier was about 84 degrees Fahrenheit, warm enough to supply plenty of heat and moisture. Winds also changed relatively little with height.

That meant there was little wind shear to tilt the storm and push its thunderstorms away from the center, allowing them to build around the same developing circulation.

Xavier also formed near the southwestern edge of a broad stretch of unusually warm water associated with El Niño.

During El Niño years, cyclones in the Southwest Pacific tend to form farther toward the central Pacific, shifting where island communities are most likely to encounter them.

Xavier developed on the eastern side of the international date line, near the northern Cook Islands.

The storm eventually reached Category 5 on the scale used in the South Pacific. As it moved west, it encountered drier air and stronger wind shear and began to weaken.

On Manihiki, one of the northern Cook Islands, the rain kept falling after the winds began to ease.

A resident told Pacific Media Network that some homes had lost sections of corrugated roofing and that electricity remained a concern.

The island was relying on solar power after losing its main diesel generator more than a year earlier, and the storm’s persistent cloud cover made it harder to keep batteries charged.

Emergency generators helped residents keep essential supplies cold. The island had also begun preparing well before Xavier appeared on satellite maps.

Each October, the island council begins removing hazardous coconut trees near homes and roads, a practice shaped by the damage Cyclone Martin inflicted on the northern Cook Islands in 1997.

Aqua passed over Xavier once that afternoon, catching a brief moment when the storm’s eye was in clear view.

On Manihiki, one of the most consequential features of the storm was the cloud cover that lingered after the worst winds had passed.

Image Credit: NASA Earth Observatory / Lauren Dauphin, using MODIS data.

#19880. Cracks in public health grew in 2026

Cracks in public health grew in 2026

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3194 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • In a recent development, it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines.
  • But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that this is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Public health is invisible — until it’s not.

In a recent development, it’s tough to tally the injuries or deaths that don’t happen thanks to seat belts, lead testing, smoking bans and vaccines. “It is the invisibility paradox,” states Georges Benjamin, CEO of the American Public Health Association in Washington, D.C. “We are invisible because when our best work is done, nothing happens.”.

But when disaster strikes — say, an outbreak or a pandemic — people take notice. This year’s outbreaks of measles, Ebola, hantavirus and cyclosporiasis brought recent federal reductions into focus — and exposed cracks in a system that aims to keep people healthy. For years, that system functioned “reasonably well” despite chronic underfunding, Benjamin says. “But since the Trump administration has come on board, they have really made the system at all levels much more dysfunctional.”.

In 2025, the second Trump administration instituted sweeping federal funding cuts and layoffs, dismantled the global health–focused U.S. Agency for International Development and withdrew the United States from the World Health Organization. Officials reversed some of those changes in the wake of lawsuits and public backlash. But the damage persists.

Two stalwarts of U.S. public health — the Food and Drug Administration and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention — have lost between 20 and 30 percent of their staff, due largely to layoffs and early retirements. They have had to scale back, pause or cancel crucial disease-tracking programs at home and abroad. Some CDC divisions don’t have enough staff to function. And both agencies have cut funding to the local governments and nonprofits that shoulder much of the nation’s public health work.

Combined with deep cuts to international aid, that has stymied efforts to contain infectious disease outbreaks around the world, with Ebola in particular going undetected for months, public health experts say.

It has been revealed that domestically, 2026 saw a record-breaking measles outbreak, with some 5,412 confirmed cases as of November 12. That’s more than double last year’s count, and it is the highest number of annual cases since 1991. In mid November, the Pan American Health Organization determined that measles is again endemic to the United States and has stripped the country of its elimination status.

Against a backdrop of shifting federal vaccine guidance, fewer children are receiving the MMR shot that prevents measles. Roughly 92 percent of kindergartners across the United States had gotten the vaccine in the 2025–2026 school year, down from 95 percent in the 2019–2020 school year, according to the CDC. At least 95 percent of people in a community need to be vaccinated to prevent the measles virus from sparking an outbreak.

“The fact that we are spending so much time and energy [on measles] when we have a reliable vaccine is very disconcerting,” indicates Lori Handy, a pediatric infectious diseases physician and associate director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia.

The CDC has not responded to Science News requests for an interview.

Such issues do not bode well for the future. Public health is tested during times of crisis, and the world will eventually face another pandemic, says Michael Osterholm, director of the Center for Infectious Disease Research and Policy at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “We’ve not responded [to the 2026 outbreaks] in a way that would give me confidence that the public health system … is prepared for what’s coming down the pike.”.

On the heels of multiple 2025 outbreaks, measles continued to wallop parts of the United States this year. Communities in South Carolina, Utah and Wisconsin have been among the hardest hit, with sporadic outbreaks also popping up in other states. Until August, however, none of this year’s outbreaks had turned deadly. That all changed in Pennsylvania.

About a quarter of this year’s cases stem from an outbreak in central Pennsylvania, where the virus has spread widely in communities with low vaccination rates. Since April, seven people in the state have died, including two infants too young to be vaccinated. The CDC has so far attributed just six deaths to measles, despite the insistence of Pennsylvania state public health officials. Three children died of measles in November in Fresh York and Wisconsin.

As of November 12, U.S. health officials recorded 5,412 measles cases for 2026. The last time this many cases were recorded was 1991, nearly a decade before the disease was eliminated from the country.

It has been revealed that measles spreads like wildfire, and one sick person can infect more than a dozen others in an unvaccinated community. While milder symptoms include fever and a hallmark full-body rash, infection can lead to pneumonia, brain swelling and even death. Statistically, the virus kills one to three out of every 1,000 infected people.

The United States eliminated measles in 2000, thanks to the MMR vaccine. “Elimination” means the virus was not spreading widely, and any outbreaks were controlled within a year. But dropping vaccination rates have reestablished the conditions to sustain multiple outbreaks — and may have done so as early as 2022, researchers reported in August in Nature Medicine.

Sources indicate that in the wake of losing measles elimination status in November, beating back the the virus again “will take a true change in the public’s trust of health care,” Handy states. That means figuring out how to get people vaccinated — and to encourage them to work with public health officials on testing and contact tracing after exposure.

During the 2009–2010 school year, 20 states had MMR vaccination rates equal to or above 95 percent among kindergartners. Just 10 states hit that threshold for 2025–2026, and 18 states had vaccination rates below 90 percent.

It has been more than three decades since measles caused widespread outbreaks in the United States, and many have never experienced the devastation it can cause. When one community hears about an outbreak halfway across the country, “it still feels very foreign,” Handy indicates. When the threat feels far away, people are not likely to line up to get a vaccine. Yet measles is so contagious that one unvaccinated traveler can bring the virus back home and spark an outbreak in their own community.

In a recent development, even with the recent spike in cases, there is hope vaccination rates can catch up, states Cornell University epidemiologist Ana Bento. She points to California and Upcoming York, which experienced outbreaks in 2015 and 2018; they ended non-medical exemptions for school vaccinations shortly thereafter. Both states now have vaccination rates above 95 percent in kindergartners. “This is not a tipping point where there’s no coming back,” Bento says.

If measles exposed the consequences of long-simmering vaccine hesitancy, then this summer’s cyclosporiasis outbreak was a quick lesson in food safety screening.

In June, Michigan detected its first cases of the foodborne illness. By August 31, contaminated lettuce had caused the largest outbreak of explosive diarrhea ever in the United States, with 12,883 cases reported across 21 states. By the time the CDC declared the outbreak over on September 11, some 570 people had been hospitalized and two had died. Another 8,113 cyclosporiasis infections have not been traced back to any source. “[This] was one of those events where you felt like the cracks showed,” Handy indicates.

But it isn’t easy to track the origins of foodborne illness. Typically, local and state public health officials report cases to the CDC — and investigate the outbreak, with the agency lending support as needed. If patient interviews reveal the culprit to be produce, dairy or packaged food, the CDC contacts the FDA, which identifies the producer and the distribution area — and coordinates recalls. The FDA also conducts on-the-ground investigations at the farms and processing facilities that supplied the food.

It can take weeks to identify which contaminated foods are behind a foodborne illness outbreak. Each outbreak is different and timing can depend on the pathogen, laboratory evidence and availability of records, an FDA spokesperson told Science News. After Michigan health officials notified CDC that something was amiss on June 25, it was another 21 days before federal officials announced a possible culprit: shredded lettuce ultimately traced to a Taylor Farms processing facility in Mexico.

Of more than 20,000 cyclosporiasis cases reported this year, nearly 13,000 occurred across 21 states, with the preponderance of them in the Midwest.

Industry observers note that the FDA aims to complete investigations as soon as possible. But delays in agency reporting early in the investigation led to unnecessary confusion about which foods to avoid in which states, said Sarah Sorscher, director of regulatory affairs at the Washington, D.C.–based Center for Science in the Public Interest, at a July 16 news briefing. “It’s a perfect storm for viral news. A lot of people have been posting on social media about avoiding fruits and vegetables, which is not good public health messaging.”.

According to recent reports, sorscher applauded the dedication of public servants working to contain the outbreak. But she remarked they were working with inadequate support. “These programs are completely overwhelmed by the scale and scope of the work of solving and communicating these novel emerging outbreaks with a dwindling set of resources.”.

Due in part to funding squeezes, in 2025 the CDC stopped mandatory surveillance of six foodborne pathogens, including the single-celled parasite that causes cyclosporiasis, Cyclospora. Speaking at the July 16 news briefing, epidemiologist Barbara Kowalcyk of George Washington University’s Institute for Food Safety and Nutrition Security in Washington, D.C., noted that half of CDC’s food safety budget goes to states to support surveillance and other programs. Yet that budget has remained flat for nearly a decade.

It has been revealed that FDA investigations have also been impacted, with foreign food inspections at historical lows. In the case of cyclosporiasis, delays gathering testing supplies and getting clearance from the Mexican government meant it took nearly a month for FDA investigators to arrive in Mexico once the source of the outbreak was identified, according to the Upcoming York Times. Once there, inspectors found the parasite in a wastewater tank at a Taylor Farms processing plant — and in a drainage ditch at a farm that supplied the lettuce. Since Cyclospora infects only humans, the probable contaminant was sewage from a source that has yet to be identified.

Industry observers note that without knowing the source of the contamination, it’s hard to know how to stop the parasite from reaching produce in the future, notes Francisco Diez-Gonzalez, a food microbiologist at the University of Georgia in Athens. “It leaves us with the feeling that we most likely are going to have something similar next year.”.

Starting in 2027, FDA aims to increase surveillance of produce historically associated with Cyclospora and boost laboratory capacity in Mexico to speed up investigations.

Outbreaks of other foodborne pathogens — including Salmonella, Listeria and E. coli — have popped up this year, but not at a rate that’s out of the ordinary, claims Diez-Gonzalez, who served on the U.S. National Advisory Committee on Microbiological Criteria for Foods before the Trump administration disbanded it in 2025. That suggests the sky isn’t falling, though he and others are concerned about our future ability to quickly contain outbreaks.

Recent findings suggest that “We may see [fewer] cases, but it’s not that they are disappearing,” Diez-Gonzalez says. “We will not be able to detect them because we don’t have the resources.”.

Sources indicate that when the WHO announced in May that an Ebola outbreak had erupted in the Democratic Republic of Congo, the virus had been simmering for months. People in the mining town of Mongbwalu, where the outbreak was first detected, began falling ill in January or earlier, according to reporting from Science. Armed conflict in the region has made the outbreak response difficult, says the WHO, and some aid workers and health facilities have been attacked.

It has been revealed that confirmed Ebola cases as of November 15, 2026. To date, 5,593 people have died, and 3,109 have recovered.

In a recent development, as cases and death counts soared in May, health officials scrambled to test a backlog of patient samples for Bundibugyo virus, the species behind what has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded. As of November 15, there were 11,432 confirmed cases and 5,593 deaths. Roughly 3,109 people have recovered. Cases have also been detected in France, Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria.

Before the outbreak, the United States significantly scaled back international aid that once flowed from USAID and the CDC. Such cuts may have hampered Ebola monitoring before the outbreak was declared — and affected infection control measures such as contact tracing, says infectious disease physician Krutika Kuppalli of UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas.

Recent findings suggest that kuppalli led an Ebola treatment unit in Sierra Leone during the 2014–2016 outbreak, the largest ever recorded. At the time, the CDC sent 1,450 physicians, epidemiologists and other experts to help out in affected areas. So far around 500 CDC employees stationed in the United States and abroad have responded to the current outbreak.

By September, the U.S. State Department pledged $887 million toward the purchase of personal protective equipment and the building of newly introduced Ebola treatment units. That’s roughly a third of the total amount sent during the 2014–2016 outbreak. Still, earlier investments in public health could have saved lives and helped minimize transmission, Kuppalli states.

Information-sharing has also been a huge problem, Kuppalli says. Prior to the second Trump administration, U.S. health officials were in constant contact with WHO teams that shared information about cases and contact-tracing efforts. After the United States withdrew from the WHO in January 2025, CDC officials had to coordinate with other groups such as UNICEF, the United Nations Children’s Fund.

In a recent development, nevertheless, there has been some progress toward developing treatments and vaccines. Researchers in Congo are testing whether antivirals and engineered antibodies can stave off severe disease and death in people infected with Bundibugyo virus, and whether those treatments can protect people after exposure. In October, a large clinical trial began testing a vaccine that is already approved against the species that caused the 2014–2016 outbreak. Kuppalli and colleagues argued in September in the Lancet Infectious Diseases that the vaccine’s potential for cross-protection merited its use in high-risk situations.

Two Bundibugyo-specific vaccines are poised to join the new trial after early evidence in animals and people showed the shots are safe — and suggested they may be protective.

Conditions have improved in some parts of Congo, according to the WHO. But there are still hundreds of new cases per week, and other countries should be prepared to respond promptly if the virus crosses borders. “The longer this outbreak continues, the more opportunities the virus has to reach new communities,” Kuppalli notes.

The M.V. Hondius was in for a rough voyage the moment it set off from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1. A passenger on the small ship had contracted Andes hantavirus, a rodent-borne disease that can cause severe respiratory illness and death. By the time the outbreak was contained, 13 people were infected and three people had died. Public health experts say a lagging U.S. response let other countries take the lead — and suggests the country is not prepared for future epidemics.

It has been revealed that it’s unclear how the first patient, who died on April 11, was infected. Another patient died on the ship, and a third — who was allowed to board a plane — died in South Africa.

More than 300 high-risk contacts, including people who spent more than 15 minutes with an infected individual, were quarantined and monitored across 33 countries and territories. None of them got sick. Nor did another 336 low-risk contacts who had brief encounters with someone who fell ill, and who monitored themselves for symptoms.

Recent findings suggest that the United States’ severed relationship with the WHO “in many ways hampered the [country’s] hantavirus outbreak response,” notes Benjamin, of the American Public Health Association. Before 2025, U.S. experts frequently received information about emerging health threats from the organization. But confusion over who government officials could talk to likely resulted in knowledge gaps and communication delays, Benjamin says. “CDC was not engaged as early on as they needed to be on that outbreak.”.

In a recent development, instead, other countries including Spain, South Africa, Argentina and Chile played leading roles. After scientists in South Africa determined that Andes hantavirus was behind the outbreak on May 2, passengers disembarked in mid-May in Tenerife, Spain, where health officials screened for symptoms and helped people travel home.

“Outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist.”.

The CDC didn’t set up a response team until after May 2, according to the Upcoming York Times. And controversy erupted over uneven U.S. quarantine practices, with some people forced to remain for weeks in quarantine units in Omaha, Neb., while others remained at home. “There was nothing standard” about the protocols, Osterholm notes. “Almost everybody got a different approach.”.

The outbreak, which ended July 2, was quickly contained in part because Andes hantavirus isn’t very contagious. Of more than 50 known hantaviruses, Andes hantavirus is the only one known to spread from person to person. Although some rare superspreaders transmit the virus to others through casual contact, transmission typically happens through close contact, such as spending long periods of time together or kissing. It would have been harder to stop a pathogen that spreads easily through the air, Osterholm indicates. “By the time that they recognized what was going on, transmission would have already occurred.”.

The international collaboration had some successes, notes virologist Gustavo Palacios of the Icahn School of Medicine at Mount Sinai in Upcoming York City. Experts in South Africa “kept digging when everything was negative,” he says, until they finally identified Andes hantavirus as the cause.

It has been revealed that hantavirus infections are also relatively rare in the Americas, for now. Studies suggest climate change will increase the likelihood that hantaviruses — and other zoonotic illnesses like Ebola — will make the jump from animals to humans. Dense cities can make it easier for diseases to spread. And such threats don’t disappear when funding for studying them dries up.

“The strongest lesson [from the M.V. Hondius] is that outbreak response depends on the knowledge and the relationships that already exist before the event,” Palacios says. Of the billions of viruses on Earth, just a few hundred pose threats to people. With enough resources, researchers can work together to learn as much as possible about those pathogens and be better prepared when a newly introduced one emerges — just as previous work on coronaviruses made the rollout of COVID-19 vaccines possible within a year of the pandemic’s start.

It has been revealed that “We will not always know in advance which [pathogens] will become vital,” Palacios indicates. But by not tracking rare threats that could one day become larger problems, “we are shooting ourselves in the foot.”.

#19879. When should women start thinking about heart disease? Earlier than you might expect

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1260 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When should women start thinking about heart disease? Earlier than you might expect

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1260 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.
  • Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.
  • Yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

New guidance explains how first periods, pregnancy complications, and menopause can offer clues to a woman’s heart disease risk.

Picture a heart attack and you probably picture a man in his fifties clutching his chest.

Yet heart disease kills more women in the U.S. than breast cancer and lung cancer combined, and much of what sets a woman’s risk happens decades before menopause.

Upcoming joint guidance from four medical societies tells doctors to start reading that risk at a girl’s first period.

The guidance comes as three papers from the American Heart Association, the American Academy of Pediatrics, the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists and the Society for Maternal-Fetal Medicine.

It’s built from existing evidence rather than a latest trial, so it reorganizes what doctors already know instead of adding a new finding.

In a recent development, sadiya Khan, a cardiologist at Northwestern University’s Feinberg School of Medicine, chaired the writing group. In an interview with Earth.com, she compared it to saving money.

It has been revealed that “You would never wait until retirement to start saving. We should bring that same thinking to heart health,” Khan said.

Standard cardiovascular risk calculators already account for sex, but they don’t capture every risk factor tied to a woman’s reproductive history.

Sources indicate that the newly introduced framework splits a woman’s life into four stages set by her hormones. They are the years around the first period, the decades of regular cycles, the transition into menopause, and the years after it.

Pregnancy counts as a separate event, running from 12 months before conception to 12 months after delivery.

Estrogen and progesterone act on blood vessels, heart muscle and the brain, not only on the reproductive organs.

Because those hormones rise and fall about once a month, with no equivalent in men, blood vessel function and sleep vary in the same rhythm.

The authors wrote that risk in each stage is shaped by the stages before it.

Asked by Earth.com which stage is most overlooked, Khan remarked the biggest gaps are what happened earlier, such as irregular or heavy periods, pregnancy complications and a diagnosis like endometriosis.

Those shape heart health in later stages, she mentioned, and belong in the conversation at every visit.

In a recent development, “Heart health for women doesn’t start at menopause,” stated Amanda Perak, a pediatric cardiologist at Lurie Children’s Hospital of Chicago who worked on all three papers. “Puberty is a big turning point.”.

A first period before age 10 is linked to higher heart disease risk later in life, and the 2026 cholesterol guideline already lists it as a risk enhancer.

Industry observers note that some irregularity is normal in the first one to three years. A pattern that persists can signal the hormone disorder that used to be called polycystic ovary syndrome, which often comes with insulin resistance and unhealthy cholesterol.

The disorder, now called polyendocrine metabolic ovarian syndrome, affects an estimated 10% to 13% of women.

Heavy periods affect 20% to 30% of young women, and about half of those with heavy bleeding are low on iron. The authors wrote that menstrual patterns may be the earliest sign of heart risk a doctor can see.

Industry observers note that mental health turns in the same years. By about age 17, girls have at least twice the odds of a depression diagnosis as boys.

In a recent development, teens with depression are more likely to develop obesity later, and the reverse holds too. Nearly one in five girls in organized sports consider quitting over menstrual concerns, the authors wrote.

“The goal isn’t to worry teens about the chance of a heart attack, which are decades away for nearly all of them,” Perak said.

“It’s that the teen years are when patterns get set, and it’s much easier to keep good heart health than to get it back.”.

Estrogen levels in pregnancy rise to about 30 times their peak in a normal cycle, and the heart and metabolism both change to support the fetus.

The authors call it a stress test because it can expose risk that was already there.

Nearly nine in ten women ages 20 to 44 begin pregnancy with less-than-ideal heart health.

High blood pressure in pregnancy, gestational diabetes and preterm birth are each linked to higher heart disease risk later in life.

Mood and anxiety disorders affect up to 37% of women in the first three months after delivery.

Sources indicate that the year after a birth is a vulnerable time for follow-up. Women move from obstetric care back to primary care, and that handoff is often missed.

The guidance notes that the obstetric threshold for hypertension, a systolic reading of at least 140 or a diastolic reading of at least 90, matches the cutoff for stage 2 hypertension in general adult care.

Perimenopause begins at a median age of about 47 in the U.S., and the authors describe it as a period of swings rather than a steady decline.

Recent findings suggest that LDL, the so-called bad cholesterol, rises during the transition independent of aging. Hot flashes affect 50% to 80% of women in this stage, and about one in three report significant depression or anxiety symptoms.

Women then spend about 40% of their lives after menopause. Around 67 million American women are 50 or older, and an estimated 6,000 more reach menopause every day.

Menopause that arrives early carries extra heart risk of its own.

Hormone therapy can help manage menopause symptoms, but the authors advise against using it to prevent heart disease.

Years of unhealthy habits may begin to show in this stage as heart disease. Stacey Rosen, the association’s immediate past volunteer president, said it is never too late to do something about it.

“It’s always about opportunities,” Rosen remarked.

A woman may see a pediatrician, a primary care doctor, an obstetrician, a cardiologist and a psychologist over her life, and their notes rarely travel with her.

One of the three papers surveyed 70 leaders of women’s cardiovascular centers and heard back from 33.

Of those programs, 29 are in cities and one is rural, and the paper proposes a national network of centers that combine the specialties.

Khan told Earth.com the papers are a first step toward giving every clinician the same playbook.

The next change, she said, is connecting all the clinicians on a woman’s care team through the life stage framework.

Industry observers note that her advice for the next appointment was a single question. “Ask at every life stage: What is my heart risk, and what should I do about it now? It is never too early to talk about your heart health,” she mentioned.

The framework rests on evidence that links these stages to risk, and the papers say plainly where the links are weakest.

Industry observers note that it isn’t known whether treating severe hot flashes lowers heart disease risk, with or without hormones. Female-specific cutoffs for heart imaging tests aren’t yet in guidelines.

And none of the three papers reports a trial showing that sorting care by life stage, rather than by age, prevents more heart attacks and strokes.

Khan said she is especially interested in reaching younger women now that risk can be estimated up to 30 years ahead with the association’s PREVENT equations.

Whether clinics can be rebuilt around that forecast is the test the four societies have set themselves.

The research was published in the journal Circulation.

  • In a recent development, massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case.
  • According to recent reports, as Rep.
  • A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

According to recent reports, as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

In a recent development, rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie said his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he said, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

Industry observers note that the petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

In a recent development, the bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

The new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Now that the upcoming petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

According to recent reports, other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the issue in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie stated. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

#19874. Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (960 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Why did Earth stay hot for millions of years? Fossil shells offer a clue

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (960 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.
  • The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.
  • Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A weaker carbon pump in the Southern Ocean may explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide during an ancient warm period.

The Southern Ocean helps move carbon from the atmosphere into the deep sea.

Around 50 million years ago, during one of Earth’s warmest periods in the past 66 million years, that process appears to have weakened.

Chemical traces in fossil shells suggest that microscopic plants at the ocean’s surface used a smaller share of the nutrients available to them than they did in cooler periods before and after.

That left more carbon dioxide in the atmosphere, according to the study’s model.

The model suggests that the weaker carbon pump and the feedbacks it amplified could explain about half of the rise in atmospheric carbon dioxide at the time.

Sources indicate that simone Moretti of the Max Planck Institute for Chemistry in Mainz, Germany, led the study. His co-authors came from the Université libre de Bruxelles (ULB), the University of California, Santa Cruz and other institutions.

“Our study highlights that the Southern Ocean played a major role in regulating atmospheric CO2 during the early Eocene, millions of years before the onset of the recent ice ages,” Moretti said.

The Early Eocene Climatic Optimum ran from about 53 to 49 million years ago. Global temperatures were more than 18°F (10°C) higher than now, and carbon dioxide reached around 1,600 parts per million.

It has been revealed that the causes of those levels are still debated. Volcanoes and reduced burial of organic carbon have both been proposed, but the timing of the eruptions lines up poorly with the warming.

So the team looked at the ocean’s biological carbon pump. Microscopic plants near the surface take up carbon dioxide as they grow. When they die, some of that carbon sinks and stays in the deep ocean for hundreds to thousands of years.

Today the pump runs below its full potential. Deep water rising around Antarctica brings up nutrients that the plants never fully use.

Plankton prefer the lighter form of nitrogen when they take up nitrate, their main nutrient. The more completely they use the supply, the heavier the leftover nitrogen becomes.

The nitrogen signature ends up in the shells of foraminifera, single-celled organisms that eat the plankton. The team measured the nitrogen trapped in fossil foraminifera from four sediment cores drilled by the Ocean Drilling Program.

It has been revealed that two cores came from the Southern Ocean. Two came from the mid-latitude Atlantic and Indian oceans, where nutrients are used up almost completely.

The gap between the two pairs of sites shows how much nutrient the Southern Ocean plants left behind. It was widest exactly when temperatures and carbon dioxide peaked, and it narrowed or vanished before and after.

The team then ran a simple model of the ocean and atmosphere using the estimated 40% drop in the share of available nutrients that plankton used.

On its own, the drop raised carbon dioxide from 700 to about 900 parts per million.

When the researchers included the effects of warming and changes in seawater chemistry, atmospheric carbon dioxide reached about 1,100 parts per million.

That increase accounts for about half of the roughly 800 parts per million rise reconstructed for the period.

It has been revealed that the leak hit harder than it would today. Eocene seawater was more acidic and richer in calcium, so it had less capacity to absorb a change in carbon dioxide.

“Because Eocene seawater had a much lower capacity to buffer changes in CO2 than today’s ocean, a weakening of the biological carbon pump could have had a far greater impact on atmospheric CO2 than under present-day conditions,” noted François Fripiat, a co-author at ULB.

Over millions of years, rain and rock weathering normally pull carbon dioxide back out of the air and act as a thermostat.

The early Eocene had no Alps or Himalayas yet, and its flat, deeply weathered continents offered little fresh rock.

“With Earth’s natural thermostat operating less efficiently, the additional CO2 released from the ocean could remain in the atmosphere for much longer,” said Mathis Hain, a co-author at the University of California, Santa Cruz.

“This would allow the Southern Ocean to influence climate not just over thousands of years, as during the ice ages, but over millions of years,” he stated.

The Southern Ocean also released carbon dioxide during warm spells between recent ice ages.

The authors interpret the match across very different timescales as a sign of a dependable feedback.

The shells record that the plants left nutrients unused, but not why. Stronger mixing around Antarctica could have brought up more deep water, or the plants could have grown less.

The authors argued that iron supply, which limits plant growth there today, likely changed little in a warmer world. That leaves less room for the growth explanation.

The estimate of the nutrient drop is deliberately conservative, because one of the mid-latitude sites falls between the others in its values.

And the carbon model is a simple one, built to show the size of the effect rather than reproduce the Eocene ocean.

The open question is whether the modern Southern Ocean will respond the same way.

Simulations run for centuries to thousands of years suggest deep-water formation near Antarctica strengthens once the deep ocean catches up with surface warming, which would match the Eocene pattern.

It has been revealed that the team is now exploring the same feedback in other periods of sustained warming. The paper names the Middle Eocene, the Middle Miocene and the Pliocene as candidates.

The full study was published in the journal Nature Geoscience.
