At the Races: Regional realignment

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1914 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.
  • Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout.
  • It has been revealed that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming England is the ancestral home of moderate Republicans, from the Saltonstalls to the Bushes, whose fiscal conservatism and social moderation defined the national GOP for decades.

Last week, Yankee Republicans suffered a near-total wipeout. Maine’s Susan Collins, Latest England's last GOP senator, lost her seat to Democrat Troy Jackson, leaving former Maine Gov. Paul LePage, who just won a House seat, as the lone Republican headed to Congress from the region. (The picture was a bit brighter at the state level, where GOP Govs. Phil Scott of Vermont and Kelly Ayotte of New Hampshire were both reelected.).

It has been revealed that one Republican operative sees a path out of the wilderness in a post-Trump era. In an opinion piece in The Boston Globe, consultant Kristin Tate urged Upcoming England Republicans to focus on fiscal discipline and recognize that “independence from national party leadership can be a political asset, not an act of betrayal.”.

After all, as the midterm election results remind us, no political realignment lasts forever.

Industry observers note that three decades ago, there were plenty of moderate Democrats from Southern states serving in Congress, governor’s mansions and even the White House. But in the years since Bill Clinton's exit from the political stage, Democrats have largely written off the South.

Which is partly why last week’s Democratic wins in the Carolinas, Georgia and, perhaps most notably, Mississippi were so stunning. All the elements that powered the party to victory nationally – disillusionment with Donald Trump, a rise in economic populism and hunger for change – played a role in the South as well.

But other factors were unique to a region that has seen renewed attempts to dilute Black political power with the redrawing of House districts to favor the GOP.

The Republican redistricting gambit in Southern states did not fully yield the desired results and seems to have helped galvanize Black voters and their allies, powering Democrats to unlikely victories.

It’s too soon to say whether the GOP’s reduced hold on the South represents a temporary blip or an enduring shift.

But Joe Trippi, a longtime Democratic strategist who advised candidates in Alabama and Florida this year, has a message for his party: “We need to invest in the South.”.

According to recent reports, #MSSEN: Democrat Scott Colom defeated GOP Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction and the first in his party to win a Senate seat in the Magnolia State since 1982.

Tar Heel tidal wave: Democrats in North Carolina have picked up at least five House seats, a striking development given the steep structural disadvantages the party faced. Prior to last week, no House Republican incumbent had lost a general election in the state since Republicans won control of the redistricting process more than a decade ago. And the Democratic gains could grow: In the 5th District, former journalist Chuck Hubbard narrowly leads 11-term Republican Rep. Virginia Foxx, and in the 3rd District, former state Rep. Raymond Smith holds a razor-thin edge over Republican Rep. Greg Murphy. The Associated Press had not called either race at publication time, though Murphy has conceded.

Republicans pick campaign chairs: Ohio Sen. Bernie Moreno and Georgia Rep. Brian Jack will be the chairs of Republicans’ respective campaign committees for the 2028 cycle. GOP lawmakers held their leadership elections Tuesday, as our colleagues Savannah Behrmann and John T. Bennett reported. Senate Republicans are sticking with South Dakota’s John Thune to lead them in the next Congress, while House Republicans picked former Freedom Caucus Chair Jim Jordan as their leader.

In a recent development, redistricting doubts: Maryland could be getting a new congressional map after voters approved a constitutional amendment that would clear the way for new lines in 2028. Our colleague Victor Feldman has more on the result and other election-related ballot measures across the country. But it’s not clear how many other states may look to redistrict next cycle after Republican efforts over the past 18 months largely didn’t pay off in last week’s elections.

Recent findings suggest that run the table: With Rep. Darren Soto winning a sixth term in Florida, no Democratic incumbent lost reelection to a Republican this year. Soto’s win in a redrawn district also meant that Florida Democrats defended all four seats the GOP had targeted under a fresh congressional map.

Industry observers note that california contest: Rep. Ken Calvert defeated fellow Republican Rep. Young Kim in a rare member-versus-member contest for a redrawn Southern California seat that turned acrimonious. Republicans are poised to hold just four House seats in the Golden State after Democrats made good on five pickup opportunities under a new congressional map.

Cheesecake Factory caucus: The latest episode of the Political Theater podcast, hosted by Roll Call editor-in-chief Jason Dick, breaks down how candidates in both parties fared in counties where The Cheesecake Factory operates, after the popular chain restaurant became something of a side character in the closing weeks of the midterm campaign.

Back to school: Newly elected members of Congress are on Capitol Hill this week for freshman orientation, an experience Massachusetts Rep.-elect Dan Koh told our colleague Nina Heller is “like high school – but it’s fun high school.” The incoming lawmakers took their class photo Thursday morning and will get to pick their Capitol Hill offices after next week’s famed lottery, Nina writes.

Tracking the count: As of 4:30 p.m. Eastern time Thursday, House Democrats had flipped 44 seats, while Republicans had picked up three. Twelve races remain uncalled, including a pair in Louisiana that will be decided by December runoffs. On the Senate side, Democrats have flipped eight seats, with only Alaska’s race still undecided.

Recent findings suggest that guv patch: Democrats flipped at least five governorships last week and will hold a majority of governor’s mansions next year. Two gubernatorial races remain uncalled by the AP: Kansas, where Democratic state Sen. Cindy Holscher is narrowly ahead of Republican state Senate President Ty Masterson, and Alaska, where Democratic former state Rep. Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is just below the 50 percent threshold to win the election outright. In territorial elections, Republicans flipped the governor’s office in Guam while voters in the Northern Mariana Islands will pick their next governor in a Nov. 20 runoff.

#TNSEN: Republican Sen. Marsha Blackburn, who was elected Tennessee governor last week, is poised to pick her Senate successor. According to the Nashville Banner, the short list includes Knox County Mayor Glenn Jacobs, a former professional wrestler, Reps. Tim Burchett and Chuck Fleischmann, and Tennessee Deputy Gov. Stuart McWhorter.

2028 on the brain: A handful of House Democrats are already considering 2028 Senate bids, according to Axios, including Kansas’ Sharice Davids, North Carolina’s Don Davis and Pennsylvania’s Chris DeLuzio.

According to recent reports, senator Morrison? Minnesota Rep. Kelly Morrison is earning buzz as a potential appointee to fill the Senate seat that Democrat Amy Klobuchar is vacating to become governor, Semafor reports. House Democrats aren’t likely to be as concerned about open seats as their Republican counterparts were in recent years, given the size of the incoming Democratic majority.

Recent findings suggest that AOC’s future: Progressive activists have introduced a new organization to encourage New York Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez to run for president in 2028. Meanwhile, Axios reports that Ocasio-Cortez has parted ways with the digital fundraising firm she’s worked with for several years and has brought on the same firm that Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders used during his two presidential campaigns.

Women lead: Shirley Emehelu is Newly introduced Jersey’s new lieutenant governor after Democratic Gov. Mikie Sherrill picked her to succeed Dale Caldwell, who resigned in September amid sexual harassment allegations and other ethical lapses. New Jersey is now one of five states to have women in both the governor’s and lieutenant governor’s offices, along with Massachusetts, Arkansas, Iowa and Virginia. Iowa will come off the list next year after an all-male Democratic ticket swept this year’s gubernatorial race, though five other states elected women to both offices last week.

According to recent reports, congress will once again be filled with losers – i.e, new members who have lost previous bids for elected office. Roll Call elections analyst Nathan L. Gonzales of Inside Elections returns to his biennial tradition as he runs down the latest list of “losers.”.

Ducking the wave: Democrats notched big wins in unexpected places, but one state grew redder after last week’s elections. The Newly introduced York Times checks in with voters in South Dakota, where the GOP won all nine statewide elections.

Here come the MBAs: Democrats with corporate connections were among the winners in last week’s elections, countering the idea that candidates with serious business credentials have struggled within the party, The Wall Street Journal reports. The field of 19 winners with M.B.A. degrees includes Costco board member Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who won the Rhode Island governor’s race, and Paige Cognetti, a Goldman Sachs alum who flipped a House seat in Pennsylvania.

It has been revealed that how Ricketts did it: Nebraska Sen. Pete Ricketts’ election night success was one of the few bright spots for the GOP. Ricketts fended off a challenge from independent Dan Osborn by painting him as a Democrat, questioning his authenticity and highlighting leaked audio of his comments denigrating Trump voters, writes the Nebraska Examiner.

Was it necessary? California redrew its congressional map to favor Democrats in response to Texas taking a similar step to boost the GOP. But some are questioning whether the state needed to cast aside its independent redistricting commission to rejigger the lines, given the scale of Democrats’ wins. “What they were literally saying is, ‘Let’s undo democracy to protect democracy,’” Lincoln Project co-founder Mike Madrid told CalMatters. “There’s something very Orwellian about it.”.

Song of the cycle: The Fresh York Times reviews “Talafreako,” an unlikely viral anthem celebrating the newly elected Democratic senator from Texas.

History does rhyme: An opinion piece in The (Charleston) Post & Courier argues that the win by Democratic Sen.-elect Annie Andrews is the latest in a long line of cases in which South Carolina voters bucked the idea of party bosses picking their leaders.

The man behind the grill: The Latest York Times profiles Russ Hudson, the Mississippi man in Colom’s now-legendary “Pick another protein” ad.

That was the last time Democrats won 11 House seats in North Carolina.

As of Thursday afternoon, they appear on track to match that number. They’ve already won nine seats – a mark they last cleared in the 1982 midterms – and they’re narrowly ahead in two more races.

It has been revealed that if those leads hold, Democrats' 11-member delegation would look much different than the one sworn in some 66 years ago in 1961. Tar Heel Democrats taking office in January would include four women, six Black members and one Hispanic member.

Their 11 representatives (out of 12) in the 87th Congress were all white men who consistently voted to uphold racial segregation and oppose major federal civil rights legislation.

Vote counting in Alaska is expected to conclude by Wednesday, Nov. 18, the targeted date for ranked choice tabulations in races in which no candidate took more than 50 percent of the vote. As of Thursday, Democratic former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan in the Senate race, though she’s below the 50 percent threshold.

Meanwhile, Democrats are gathering in Denver beginning Thursday to celebrate their historic wins and plot their next steps.

Industry News: An El Niño amped by climate change has California bracing for the worst

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2182 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready.
  • What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves.
  • Industry observers note that californians know all too well the threat.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in parts of California, public officials are going door-to-door, warning residents to get ready. The state has strategically stockpiled sandbags, pumps and generators. Debris has been fished out to clear storm drains, seepage blankets shore up aging levees and dams, and wire mesh cages hold back precariously placed boulders.

What is expected to be the strongest El Niño on record is already pounding the state with giant waves. The fury of this year’s El Niño is being unleashed around the globe as well, from inundating Florida with floods to exacerbating drought in the Amazon. And much more is still to come, forecasts show, with the peak of the climate phenomenon expected to arrive between November 2026 and January 2027.

Industry observers note that californians know all too well the threat. El Niño has historically brought relentless rainfall to the state, flooding cities and triggering landslides.

State officials learned a lot about preparedness and emergency water management from previous El Niños — particularly the strong event that spanned the winter of 1997–1998. But this year’s event is likely to be even more challenging, a “Super” El Niño superimposed on the backdrop of global climate change.

Climate change has made water management in California more complicated than it was just 30 years ago — as it has elsewhere around the world, claims environmental scientist Letitia Grenier, the director of water policy at the Public Policy Institute of California, a nonprofit, nonpartisan think tank based in San Francisco.

Sources indicate that in 1997, California’s overall climate was much drier; El Niño brought a substantial, long rainy season that spanned the state, Grenier says. But now, “it’s just so humid. The air is warmer, so it can hold more water.”.

According to recent reports, that waterlogged atmosphere means that even without El Niño, there’s been less of a distinct rainy season in California, and more rapid flip-flop between intense episodes of rain dumped on the ground followed by periods of heat and dryness. “It’s these strange, erratic patterns that we’ve never seen before,” she says. And the state is bracing for how the Super El Niño will clash with this upcoming climate normal.

In a recent development, 1997 was the year that the term “El Niño” shot to global fame. It was the most powerful El Niño in recorded history, and the first to be scientifically monitored in real time, continuously tracked by satellites and breathlessly reported on by news outlets. El Niño’s rise to household name status was even cemented in pop culture by an appearance on Saturday Night Live, in a classic sketch by comedian Chris Farley.

But the event was no laughing matter. It caused global devastation during its brief reign. El Niño events form as westward-blowing trade winds over the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean weaken, allowing warm water to accumulate at the surface. Those waters can then release massive amounts of heat to the atmosphere, altering the position of the Pacific jet stream and helping to disrupt global weather patterns.

Recent findings suggest that in 1997–1998, global temperatures spiked by 1.5 degrees Celsius on average. Along with the torrential rains in California, the event brought brutal drought to Southeast Asia and deadly summer floods to central Europe and Peru. Record-breaking floods also hit East Africa, which in turn triggered a surge in mosquito-borne Rift Valley fever. The oceans were so warm that 16 percent of the world’s reefs died.

In all, the El Niño–related weather extremes were linked to more than 22,000 fatalities around the world, including nearly 200 in the United States, and an estimated $5.7 trillion in global economic losses.

In a recent development, not every El Niño is equally intense, or impacts weather in quite the same way. “There’s a lot of variability event to event,” notes Washington, D.C.–based climate scientist Tom Di Liberto, of the nonprofit climate news organization Climate Central.

But there is a general overall pattern to how El Niño tends to affect weather around the planet, Di Liberto states. For example, there tend to be more tropical cyclones in the Pacific Ocean, and fewer in the Atlantic — a pattern also observed in 2026.

It has been revealed that el Niño also tends to flatten and accelerate the Pacific jet stream, shifting its flow southward, says Mike Anderson, California’s state climatologist for the Department of Water Resources, who is based in Sacramento. And that has historically meant that a conveyor belt of back-to-back moisture-loaded storms is set on a collision course with the U.S. West Coast.

In a recent development, the El Niño rapidly strengthened during the summer of 2026. As westerly trade winds weakened, warm waters accumulated in the eastern tropical Pacific Ocean, raising both ocean temperatures and the sea level height (shown in this animation). Red and white colors indicate the highest sea level. Beginning in April and intensifying through November, the El Niño event generated Kelvin waves, massive swells that sweep eastward along the equator toward the Americas.

The 1997–1998 El Niño revealed just how devastating that pattern could be in California.

It has been revealed that as much as 30 centimeters inundated parts of the state during the month of February 1998 alone. Storm winds and high surf pounded the coast, while rivers swelled and overtopped their banks. Flooding from the “Groundhog Day Storm” destroyed some 1,700 homes in Bay Area cities Palo Alto and Menlo Park. On February 6 near Rio Nido, about 100 kilometers from San Francisco, a forested hillside suddenly crumbled, sending a wall of mud rushing down the mountain. It destroyed about 30 homes.

Landslides also threatened homes and lives in Southern California.

On February 23, then 25-year-old Jenifer Segraves and her fiancé Glenn Flook were living in an apartment on Laguna Canyon Road, in the city of Laguna Beach. The heavy rains had saturated the neighborhood’s steep hillsides, making the terrain unstable.

“We lived up against a hill in the canyon, so there were stairs up to our apartment,” Segraves indicates now. “They became like a waterfall. I remember my fiancé carrying me up the stairs because there was so much water.” Segraves called her father, Gary Segraves, in a panic, asking for help. Then, the slope behind the building failed, the apartment flooded and she and Flook fled into the rushing mud.

“We were strong enough to get out, but we were waist-high in mud,” Segraves noted. “[My dad] almost drowned getting to us.” All three took shelter at a neighbor’s house, where they showered and hunkered down to wait out the rain.

Around midnight on February 24, the second mudslide arrived.

In a recent development, the neighbor’s “whole house went down,” Segraves notes. She escaped through a second-floor window, but her fiancé fell through the floor and was knocked out. He didn’t make it out.

Gary Segraves, meanwhile, was swept down the hillside and landed in a pile of rubble against a rocky cliff. Battered and missing his glasses, he looked around and saw what looked like a doll.

Recent findings suggest that he reached for the little form — and discovered that it was a baby, very cold but alive. Somehow, the 9-month-old had survived being swept out of her crib from a nearby home. The little girl “wouldn’t have survived if he hadn’t picked her up,” Segraves says.

Recent findings suggest that the havoc wreaked across California by the event 30 years ago cast a stark light on the desperate need to expand waterways, maintain infrastructure and coordinate emergency services, Grenier notes. “An engineering system can only work as well as its capacity.”.

It has been revealed that much of the state’s infrastructure is deteriorating. An October 13 report by the California state auditor noted that the condition of dams and levees across the state “remains a high-risk issue,” with some 57 dams in the state in poor or unsatisfactory condition. “Poorly maintained dams and levees continue to pose a risk to public safety,” the report said.

Industry observers note that california’s water management system was also originally designed specifically to simply shunt excess water away from residential areas, rather than try to capture the water or help it infiltrate into aquifers, Grenier says. But that system worked for a different climate, one that wasn’t so prone to “weather whiplash” — wild, sudden swings between extremely wet and extremely dry conditions.

Alongside punishing, drenching back-to-back storms called atmospheric rivers, the state has also experienced frequent episodes of drought, including two recent severe events, one lasting from 2012 to 2016 and another from 2021 to 2025.

Those years of drought, dwindling snow and pumping too much water from aquifers have dramatically depleted the state’s subsurface water stores. And the heavy rains don’t necessarily help; the torrents of water mostly run off across the surface instead of infiltrating soils to reach the underground aquifer.

Such hydroclimate whiplash isn’t unique to California by any means. It’s a global problem, and it’s becoming more common. A small increase in air temperatures can give a massive boost to the atmosphere’s capacity to hold water vapor, increasing that capacity by about 7 percent for every 1 degree C of temperature increase. All of that water vapor has contributed to an increase in extreme precipitation events around the globe since the mid-20th century.

Sources indicate that precipitation is just half of the problem. Rising air temperatures also make the air “thirstier,” causing it to draw even more moisture out of vegetation, soil and surface bodies of water during drier periods — which makes the land more vulnerable to severe drought and wildfire.

It’s now clear that these hydrodynamic shifts have been increasing the frequency of weather whiplash events around the world over the last 75 years or so, scientists reported in 2025. And that whiplash is likely to increase as the world warms more.

Months before reaching peak intensity, the 2026–2027 Super El Niño has begun making its presence known. The Amazon is suffering under intense heat and drought, priming the region for wildfires and pushing the forest closer to a worrisome possible fate: a transition from tropical forest to savanna grasslands. Fires have also begun blazing across Southeast Asia, while heavy rains began inundating the Horn of Africa in October. Arriving on the heels of severe drought, that one-two punch could devastate the region’s crops and pasturelands.

Industry observers note that in California, the first harbingers of the arrival of the Super El Niño appeared in early September. Heavy surf pounded the coastline. Regions from San Francisco to Los Angeles saw record high tides by late October that flooded city streets and battered coastlines and seawalls, even as the skies remained clear.

The waves were amped up by an unfortunate trifecta: higher sea levels due to climate change; a lunar cycle that exerted its maximum pull on the tides; and an El Niño–linked phenomenon called Kelvin waves.

Kelvin waves are massive, slow-moving swells of warm ocean water, part of the complicated interplay between wind and water that produces the El Niño Southern Oscillation, the overall weather pattern that includes El Niño and counterpart La Niña events, says Josh Willis, an oceanographer at NASA’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory in Pasadena, Calif.

As prevailing west-blowing winds weaken over the tropical eastern Pacific, Willis says, water normally pushed west by the winds instead sloshes back eastward. Kelvin waves have historically given a boost to sea levels along the U.S. West Coast of as much as 30 centimeters. This year, that impact could be larger, researchers reported September 30 in a preprint study posted on EarthArXiv.org. Computer model simulations suggest that the risk of the risk of extreme sea levels could be 10 times higher during this El Niño year than during previous events, for coastlines from Alaska all the way to Chile.

Then, by late October, the Santa Ana winds arrived: Hot, dry gusts blowing down the mountains toward the coast, fanning wildfires in Southern California. The fires scarred the landscape, denuding it of vegetation, roots that helped stabilize and fortify the soil. Such loosened soil is more likely to become mobilized into a debris flow during heavy rains.

It has been revealed that those rains are now on the way. By mid-November, researchers began tracking storms headed for California. The peak of El Niño is expected to arrive by late November or early December and persist through February or March.

Industry observers note that segraves, after surviving nearly 30 years ago, indicates she is aware that another El Niño is coming. But she hasn’t been following the news closely. She’s placed herself on a news diet since her ordeal. She refused to speak to media for years, or even read the coverage about her own story.

“Everyone wanted to talk to me and I just wanted to be left alone,” she says. Staying away from the news “freed me from all that. It changed my view on life. I take each day as it comes.”.

But, she adds, one lesson has stayed with her. “I swore I would never live on a cliff again.”.
